title: Mediators of the Associations of County Poverty, County Percentage Black, and Rurality with Hospital Closure
content: Hospital closure is concentrated in some communities, but it is not known through which hospital characteristics county poverty, racial composition, and rurality are linked to closure. We analyzed Medicare cost reports for short-term acute care and critical access hospitals in the 50 states and the District of Columbia (reports of 150–365 days; 4,785 hospitals, 45,107 hospital-years, 325 closures, 2011–2020), linked to county poverty and percentage Black from the American Community Survey. A parallel multiple-mediator model with 16 mediators estimated associations with closure in the following year as risk differences per 1000 hospital-years, with a hospital-clustered bootstrap. Each standard deviation of county poverty was associated with 1.64 (95% CI 0.72, 2.60) more closures, 59% of it indirect, through critical access status, total margin, occupancy, and for-profit ownership, partly offset by larger hospital size. County percentage Black had a direct association (1.58; 0.52, 2.74) masked by opposing indirect associations (−0.83). Rural location showed no net association because pathways through smaller size and lower margins were offset by critical access status. Days cash, payer mix, charity care, and bad debt did not mediate any association. Community poverty is linked to closure mainly through margins, utilization, structure, and ownership, not uncompensated care; monitoring should address margins and occupancy.
